name: Fourier's Law of Heat Conduction
statement: Heat flux through a material is proportional to the negative of the local temperature gradient, with thermal conductivity as the constant: q = -k∇T.
meaning: Fourier's law states that heat flows from hot to cold at a rate set by how steep the temperature difference is. In the vector form q = -k∇T, q is the local heat flux density, k the thermal conductivity, and ∇T the temperature gradient. The minus sign encodes that heat moves down the gradient, toward lower temperature.
mechanism: Heat conduction transfers thermal energy through molecular and lattice interactions without bulk motion of material. In solids, atomic vibrations — and, in metals, free electrons — carry kinetic energy from hotter, more energetic regions to colder ones via collisions. The net energy transport is proportional to the steepness of the temperature gradient.

examples.text: For steady conduction through a flat wall, the flux equals −k times the temperature change over thickness, so doubling the temperature difference doubles the heat flux.
Conduction is fastest in solids and slowest in gases because closely spaced particles transmit vibrational energy more effectively.
Fourier's law is the template for a family of transport laws, directly analogous to Fick's law of diffusion, Ohm's law, and Darcy's law.

whyItMatters: It is the governing rate law for conduction and, combined with energy conservation, yields the heat equation used throughout engineering and physics. It underlies the thermal design of everything from buildings and electronics to engines and spacecraft.
limits: It is a continuum, empirical law valid when many carrier collisions occur over the length and time scales of interest. It breaks down at the nanoscale and at very short timescales, where heat transport becomes ballistic rather than diffusive and the local-gradient assumption fails; it also treats conductivity as a property that may itself depend on temperature.
misreadings: The negative sign does not mean heat flux is negative; it means flux points opposite to the temperature gradient, toward colder regions. The law describes conduction only, not convection or radiation.
origin: Joseph Fourier, first published in his 1822 book Théorie analytique de la chaleur.

sources.text: Wikipedia's article on thermal conduction, giving Fourier's law q = -κ∇T, the one-dimensional form, and the conduction mechanism — supports the statement and mechanism.

Encyclopaedia Britannica's entry on Fourier's law of heat conduction, confirming q = -k∇T with heat-transfer rate proportional to the negative temperature gradient — supports the statement and attribution.
